assignmentHtml.task: Research RisingWave's specific capabilities in depth for this architecture. Investigate: (1) its Kafka source with DEBEZIUM format — how it handles deletes, updates, out-of-order; (2) materialized views over joins with streaming sources — what happens when a dimension updates; (3) its 'strongly consistent reads' claim — how is this guaranteed via checkpoints; (4) multi-tenant isolation details — database-level isolation, resource groups, RBAC with RLS? Does it have row-level security?; (5) erasure/correction — can you DELETE rows from a materialized view source? Can you do a mass update?; (6) recovery after failure — what exactly is restored from Chandy-Lamport checkpoints; (7) stateful component count — Meta node is required; Compactor is optional. How many independently operated stateful components does a self-hosted RisingWave deployment require?
assignmentHtml.context: Evidence cutoff 2026-09-16. Workload B: mutable orders via CDC with deletes, out-of-order, schema changes. Workload D: 2000 merchants needing tenant isolation. Workload E: corrections and erasure. Workload F: max 3 stateful components beyond Kafka, PostgreSQL, object storage. RisingWave is a candidate for serving layer.
assignmentHtml.expected_output: In-depth RisingWave dossier covering CDC handling, MV semantics, consistency guarantees, multi-tenant isolation, correction/erasure support, recovery details, and stateful component count for self-hosted deployments, with source URLs.

answerHtml:
RisingWave Dossier: CDC handling, MV semantics, consistency, multi-tenant isolation, correction/erasure, recovery, and stateful component count.

1. Kafka Source with DEBEZIUM Format — Deletes, Updates, Out-of-Order

FORMAT DEBEZIUM ENCODE JSON/AVRO treats a Kafka topic as a full changelog mirroring the upstream table. RisingWave applies every insert (op='c'), update (op='u'), and delete (op='d') event to maintain a mutable upsert mirror with one row per primary key [1][2]. Tombstone (null-value) messages are automatically skipped — RisingWave does not crash on them; the preceding op='d' event drives the retraction [3]. When Debezium restarts and replays events, duplicates are handled safely via idempotent upserts [4].

For ordering, RisingWave embeds the Debezium Embedded Engine in the connector node, producing a single strictly-linear stream ordered identically to the upstream DB's commit order, complete with BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK markers — no downstream reassembly logic needed [5]. Multi-table CDC sources use one connection to subscribe to multiple tables, so all events within a transaction land in the same epoch atomically [5]. Barriers are paused during transactions to guarantee atomic visibility [5]. However, per-partition ordering follows standard Kafka semantics: ordering is guaranteed only within a partition, not globally across partitions.

Out-of-order event-time processing is handled via watermarks defined with WATERMARK FOR <col> AS <col> - INTERVAL '<delay>', which allow configurable allowed lateness for late-arriving events in windowing operations [6]. Note: watermarks apply to event-time windows/joins, not to the CDC upsert mirror itself, which is keyed by primary key.

2. Materialized Views Over Joins with Streaming Sources — Dimension Updates

Two join semantics exist:

  • Regular JOIN: Any update to a dimension table triggers recomputation of the join result for ALL matching fact rows. Correct but inefficient for fact-dimension enrichment patterns [7].
  • Process-time temporal joins (FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF PROCTIME()): Each stream event is joined with the dimension row version active at processing time. Existing MV results are locked in and unchanged when the dimension updates; new events use updated dimension values. Append-only temporal joins require no join-state maintenance; non-append-only variants maintain internal state per LHS insertion to support retractions on updates/deletes [8][7].

Without temporal joins, dimension table updates DO propagate to dependent MVs — the MV is incrementally maintained as either side of the join changes, recomputing affected results [9][10]. For pure enrichment where historical results should not change, temporal joins are required.

3. 'Strongly Consistent Reads' — Guaranteed via Checkpoints

RisingWave adopts the Chandy–Lamport algorithm to create global consistent snapshots (checkpoints) of the entire streaming system. Default barrier interval is 1 second (barrier_interval_ms=1000), meaning a checkpoint is created approximately every second [11][12].

The critical guarantee: "For read queries, data is always fetched from the last checkpoint. This ensures that the data is correct and consistent" [12]. Checkpoints persist incremental states of streaming operators and output results to durable remote object storage (S3/GCS/HDFS via OpenDAL). States are flushed on barrier processing or when memory thresholds are exceeded [11].

This means every read query sees a consistent cut — no partial or evolving state — because reads never observe the in-flight local state, only the last completed checkpoint [12].

4. Multi-Tenant Isolation Details

  • Database-level isolation (v2.3+): Independent checkpoints per database; localized job error recovery limits blast radius [13].
  • Resource groups: Named logical pools of Compute Nodes assigned at CN startup (--resource-group or RW_RESOURCE_GROUP). Databases are pinned to resource groups via CREATE DATABASE ... WITH RESOURCE_GROUP, constraining all streaming jobs to specific CNs for fault isolation and workload matching [13].
  • RBAC: User-based access control (privileges granted directly to users, not via intermediate roles). Privilege levels: Database, Schema, Table, Source, Materialized View. Available privileges: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE, CONNECT, USAGE. Authentication via password, OAuth, LDAP [14].
  • Row-Level Security (RLS): NOT natively supported. RisingWave documents achieving equivalent behavior via logical views filtered per role combined with GRANT/REVOKE access control on those views [15].
  • Cross-database queries (v2.3+): SELECT across databases using three-part naming; requires CONNECT privilege on target DB plus object-level privileges; streaming cross-database MVs require CREATE SUBSCRIPTION [13].

5. Erasure/Correction — Deleting Rows, Mass Updates

  • Cannot directly modify MVs: "Data on a materialized view cannot be directly updated or deleted by users" [16].
  • Can modify tables (including CDC-sourced tables) via SQL: UPDATE t SET ... WHERE ... and DELETE FROM t WHERE ... trigger automatic MV updates [16].
  • CDC-driven corrections: Send op='u' (update) or op='d' (delete) events through the Debezium-formatted Kafka topic. RisingWave applies these to the underlying table, and all dependent MVs are incrementally updated [1][2][3].
  • Mass updates/deletes: Supported via standard SQL DML on tables. Both operations generate changelog entries that propagate to dependent MVs [16].
  • Sources hold no data: "A source does not hold any data, so users cannot perform any update or deletion operations on a source" — changes must flow through the CDC stream or direct table DML [16].
  • Note on deletes: Deletions are represented in the changelog and do not immediately erase data from object storage; tombstones are created and reclaimed during compaction [17].

6. Recovery After Failure — What Exactly Is Restored

On failure: "All the internal stateful operators in RisingWave will fetch the states from the last checkpoint" [12]. Specifically restored:

  • All operator internal states (aggregation state, join state, buffer state) as of the last checkpoint
  • Output results captured in the checkpoint
  • Source consumer offsets (Kafka offsets persist independently)

What is NOT restored: Only states generated after the last checkpoint are lost (bounded by ~1 second at default settings). The system recomputes only from the checkpoint forward, avoiding full re-computation from ingestion start [12]. Checkpoints align with transaction boundaries because barriers are paused during transactions, so transactions are never lost or re-applied on recovery [5].

Recovery speed depends on loading checkpoint state from Hummock (remote object storage) onto recovery nodes [18].

7. Stateful Component Count — Self-Hosted Deployment

Four node types exist [19]:

Node Type Stateful? Required?
Meta Node YES (manages cluster metadata) REQUIRED (1 min, 2 recommended for HA)
Compute Node (hybrid Serving+Streaming by default) YES (maintains streaming state, owns vnodes, local Hummock state) REQUIRED (scales horizontally)
Compactor Node Operationally stateful (performs LSM-tree compaction; data ownership resides in object storage) OPTIONAL but recommended
Frontend/Serving Node NO (stateless) Optional scale-out

Minimum self-hosted deployment: 1 Meta Node + 1 Compute Node = 2 independently operated stateful components. With optional compactor: up to 3. In standalone mode, all four run embedded in a single process with embedded LocalFs and SQLite [20].

For Workload F (max 3 stateful components beyond Kafka/PostgreSQL/object storage): RisingWave fits — Meta (stateful) + Compute (stateful) + optional Compactor (stateful) = 3 maximum, with Frontend being stateless. Note: an external meta store (Postgres/MySQL/SQLite) is also required, but this falls under the excluded categories.

evidence.snippet: FORMAT DEBEZIUM treats the topic as a changelog; every insert, update, and delete event is applied to maintain a live replica with one row per primary key. FORMAT PLAIN filters to insert-only events and silently drops updates/deletes.
evidence.supports: FORMAT DEBEZIUM handles inserts, updates, and deletes; creates a mutable upsert mirror

evidence.snippet: RisingWave's Kafka consumer with FORMAT DEBEZIUM ENCODE JSON skips messages with null values rather than crashing. The delete event that precedes the tombstone is what drives the retraction in materialized views.
evidence.supports: Tombstones are skipped; deletes are driven by op='d' events, no crash

evidence.snippet: RisingWave handles Debezium's op field correctly and applies idempotent upserts for c and u operations, so duplicate events are handled safely. RisingWave manages its own consumer group offset.
evidence.supports: Duplicates after Debezium restart are safe; offsets managed independently

evidence.snippet: RisingWave embeds the Debezium Embedded Engine producing a single, strictly linear stream of events whose order is identical to the commit order of the upstream database, complete with transaction markers. Barriers are paused during a transaction; buffered events are atomically flushed on COMMIT.
evidence.supports: Strict ordering per upstream commit order; cross-table transactional atomicity via barrier pausing

evidence.snippet: RisingWave uses watermarks for event-time processing. Users define watermarks via WATERMARK FOR <event_time_column> AS <event_time_column> - INTERVAL '<delay>'. Allowed lateness permits late events to still update window results.
evidence.supports: Watermarks handle out-of-order/late event-time events in windowing operations

evidence.snippet: RisingWave aims for point-in-time correctness (temporal joins). Incremental updates occur when either side of the join changes. LEFT OUTER JOIN always outputs every stream event even if dimension match is missing.
evidence.supports: Dimension updates propagate to MV joins; temporal joins lock in historical dimension values

evidence.snippet: If the fact table only needs to look up the dimension table at the time of the join, PROCESS TIME JOIN will not recompute join results when the dimension table updates. Non-append-only temporal joins maintain internal state to retract join results on update/delete messages.
evidence.supports: Regular JOIN recomputes on dimension updates; temporal joins avoid this

evidence.snippet: Incremental materialized views automatically update stored query results by computing only changes caused by new, updated, or deleted source data. RisingWave supports incremental maintenance of complex joins including multi-way joins.
evidence.supports: MVs are incrementally maintained on deletes, updates, inserts

evidence.snippet: RisingWave adopts the Chandy-Lamport algorithm to create checkpoints — a global snapshot representing a consistent state of the entire system. Default barrier interval is 1000ms; checkpoint_frequency=1. States flushed to S3/GCS/HDFS.
evidence.supports: Chandy-Lamport checkpoints every ~1 second; persisted to object storage

evidence.snippet: For read queries, data is always fetched from the last checkpoint. This ensures that the data is correct and consistent. If a failure occurs, only the states that are not saved to the upcoming checkpoint are lost. All internal stateful operators fetch states from the last checkpoint.
evidence.supports: Strong consistent reads guaranteed by always reading from last checkpoint; recovery restores all operator states from last checkpoint

evidence.snippet: Database isolation: independent checkpoints per database, localized job error recovery. Resource groups: named pools of Compute Nodes; databases assigned via CREATE DATABASE WITH RESOURCE_GROUP. Cross-database queries require CONNECT and SELECT privileges.
evidence.supports: Database-level isolation, resource groups, cross-database permissions

evidence.snippet: RisingWave uses a user-based access control model. Privileges managed at Database, Schema, Table, Source, Materialized View levels: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE, CONNECT, USAGE. No intermediate roles; privileges granted directly to users.
evidence.supports: RBAC is user-based, not role-based; available privilege set documented

evidence.snippet: While RisingWave does not natively support Row Security Policies, you can achieve equivalent row-level security through a combination of logical views with access control.
evidence.supports: RLS not natively supported; workaround via filtered logical views + GRANT/REVOKE

evidence.snippet: Data on a table can be updated or deleted... A source does not hold any data, so users cannot perform any update or deletion operations on a source. Data on a materialized view cannot be directly updated or deleted by users. When data in a table is modified or deleted, any materialized views built on that table will be updated accordingly.
evidence.supports: MV cannot be directly modified; corrections flow through underlying table DML or CDC; MVs auto-update

evidence.snippet: Node types: Serving Node (stateless, PostgreSQL-compatible frontend), Streaming Node (stateful, maintains streaming job state), Meta Node (central coordinator, manages metadata), Compactor Node (background LSM-tree compaction). Compute Node can be dedicated Serving, dedicated Streaming, or hybrid (default).
evidence.supports: Serving/frontend is stateless; streaming/compute and meta are stateful; compactor is background

evidence.snippet: It is advisable to deploy 2 Meta Nodes (primary and backup) to ensure faster recovery and avoid single points of failure. Frontend Nodes are stateless. Compactor Nodes perform background compaction; insufficient resources result in slow state access.
evidence.supports: Meta required (2 recommended for HA); Frontend stateless; Compactor optional

evidence.snippet: RisingWave standalone mode starts the cluster as a single process. Components including serving node, streaming node, meta node, and compactor node are all embedded in this process. Uses embedded LocalFs Object Store and SQLite for meta store.
evidence.supports: Standalone mode: single process contains all four node types
